chunks: "In CMOS logic the PMOS goes on the high side and the NMOS on the low side, and the reason comes down to where the source sits. A MOSFET is controlled by gate-to-source voltage.
On the low side, the NMOS source is at ground, so putting V DD on the gate gives it the full V DD of V GS ; it turns hard on and pulls the output all the way to 0 volts.
On the high side, the PMOS source is at V DD , so pulling its gate to 0 volts gives V GS equals -V DD ; it turns hard on and pulls the output all the way to V DD .
Both are driven by the same 0-to- V DD signal.
If you swapped them, the NMOS on top would be a source follower: its source is the output, so it turns off once the output gets within a threshold of the gate, and you only get about V DD minus V t .
People say NMOS passes a strong 0 and a weak 1, and PMOS passes a strong 1 and a weak 0. In power circuits it's a bit different. The low side is still NMOS.
For the high side, a PMOS is easy to drive, but NMOS has two to three times lower on-resistance for the same size because electrons are more mobile.
So at higher currents you use an NMOS on the high side too, and pay for it with a bootstrap or charge-pump gate driver to get its gate above the supply."
